label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
To: #maintenance
Replying to: s03
Cc: none
Subject: none

Dana, yes—you can do this yourself. Allow 2–3 hours with a helper, rather than treating it as a twenty-minute job. $465 isn’t a ripoff for doing the engine and water system properly, but learning your own boat is a good reason to tackle it.

Hector, one correction before Dana buys supplies: I wouldn’t use green automotive antifreeze for this job. Ethylene glycol is toxic, and that automotive product isn’t rated for winterizing the raw-water system. Use pink propylene glycol RV/marine antifreeze specifically labeled for the intended application—potable-water use for the domestic system. Neither green nor pink belongs in the river.

Your 3GM30F has two separate cooling circuits. The closed, freshwater side circulates engine coolant through a heat exchanger. Check its strength with a hydrometer suitable for that coolant; a proper 50/50 mix generally protects to about minus 20°F. Don’t replace that coolant with pink winterizing antifreeze. The other circuit brings seawater through the engine’s raw-water equipment and out through the exhaust. That’s the side people miss, and trapped water can freeze and crack things.

Here’s the order I’d use, with the Yanmar and antifreeze manufacturers’ winterizing instructions alongside you:

1. Get supplies and arrange collection first. Figure roughly two gallons of pink for the engine and another two or three for the water system, but those are shopping estimates, not completion criteria. Buy enough to finish both procedures and verify protection. It’s around $6 a gallon at West Marine or Walmart, depending on the product. Have the oil, filter, fuel stabilizer and a spare raw-water impeller ready too. Keep a spare impeller aboard regardless.

Set up a safe way to capture the exhaust discharge before starting the engine. Your helper watches both flow and collection throughout; stop if either gets away from you. Collect all winterizing discharge for appropriate disposal ashore, including the water-system discharge.

2. Warm the engine with its normal cooling-water supply, then shut down and change the oil and filter while the oil is warm. Top up the fuel tank without overfilling, add diesel-compatible stabilizer at the labeled dose, and run about ten minutes to circulate it. Keep the cooling-water supply working normally during this running.

3. Do the raw-water winterizing last. With the engine stopped, close the intake seacock and arrange the strainer intake to draw from your antifreeze supply, following the prescribed procedure. Run at idle, keeping the pump supplied and wet the whole time. Never let it suck the container dry. Your helper watches the exhaust flow and captures it.

Follow the engine and antifreeze instructions through completion, and test the discharged mixture by the antifreeze manufacturer’s specified method to confirm the required winter protection. Pink coming out is not proof: residual water dilutes it. Shut the engine down when complete and leave the seacock closed. Tag it so it gets reopened before any normal spring start.

If you want to remove the old impeller for inspection or storage, do that afterward, following Yanmar’s instructions. Don’t run the pump dry.

4. For the domestic water system, switch off the water-heater breaker before draining anything. Leave it off until the heater is refilled in spring. Drain the heater first, then use the bypass valve behind the companionway steps on your Catalina; otherwise you’ll waste six gallons filling the heater with pink.

Drain the freshwater tank and winterize the pump, lines, and every hot and cold outlet according to the system and antifreeze instructions. Capture that discharge too, and verify protection rather than judging by color alone.

That Christmas freeze a few years back cracked exhaust elbows or strainers on three boats on C dock. All three had skipped or rushed the raw-water side. That’s where patience pays.

I can come down Saturday morning if you’d like a second set of hands. You do the job; I’ll help watch the flow and collection.
